To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
pH 4 treatment inactivates some viruses but that viral inactivation is reduced when viruses are complexed with antibody.
the treatment of human immunoglobulin preparations with low levels of acid (pH 4) and pepsin can contribute to their viral safety.
“Pepsin treatment of intravenous immunoglobin at pH 4 inactivates viruses, including viruses that have formed complexes with the antibody in immunoglobulin preparations.”
In summary, our research is concerned with
the potential contribution of mild pepsin treatment at pH 4 to the viral safety of human immunoglobulin (IVIG) products.
the potential of mild pepsin treatment at pH4 to contribute to the viral safety of intravenous immunogobulin products.
the safety of immunoglobulins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the treatment of intravenous immunoglobulin with mild pepsin at low pH (4) is an additional safety measure that contributes to the safety of the product, and that the treatment is effective against viruses that are susceptible to acid pH and inactivated at pH 4/5, but is not effective against acid‐resistant viruses.
the use of pH 4/ pepsin treatment may help to inactivate some viruses that are present in human IgG preparations.

pH 4 pepsin treatment is effective in reducing the infectivity of acid-labile viruses, such as vaccinia and Semliki forest virus, and that the presence of antibody does not significantly protect such viruses against this treatment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pH 4‐pepsin treatment of human immunoglobulin preparations may contribute to their viral safety.

the treatment of intravenous immunoglobin with pH 4/ pepsin is a useful viral inactivation step that is capable of inactivating most potential virus contaminants, including those that are acid‐labile.

the treatment of intravenous immunoglobin with pH 4 and pepsin at a low level (1/10,000 of the amount normally used) can inactivate a range viruses that are likely to contaminate intravenous immunoglobin products.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pH 4/psin treatment is effective against some viruses, but it is not effective against all viruses.
the use of pepsin in the manufacture of IVIG products is a very important safety step.
pH 4 peptic digestion is an important step in the manufacture of intravenous Ig, as it inactivates many viruses, including the acid‐stable poliovirus, which is resistant to the low pH step.
